old: Ten cents from the East Caribbean States, dated 1991 — an older brother to the 2014 steel ten cents filed the same day. The back is the same Golden Hind, Drake's little round-the-world galleon, with a 10 on each side. The front is what gives its age away: the Queen is young here, in Arnold Machin's portrait wearing a tiara, the likeness these islands used from the 1980s into the early 2000s before switching to the older crowned portrait. Eight Caribbean islands spend this one money, and coins like this crossed between them in every ferry and market stall. This one is copper-nickel, from the British Royal Mint years, heavier in the hand than the steel strikes that replaced it.

old: Both sides photographed in the holder. Reverse: EAST CARIBBEAN STATES around the Golden Hind, the date 1991 down the right rim read digit by digit in an enlarged view (1-9-9-1), a 10 on each side of the ship, TEN CENTS below. Obverse: QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND around the young Machin portrait — a different portrait generation from the collection's 2004 strikes of this denomination, which carry the crowned Rank-Broadley portrait, and from the 2014 steel strike filed beside it; that portrait is what places this coin in the 1989-2000 striking of the design. Filed as its own type (EC.X.10-cents.2) to keep the portrait generations apart, following the collection's existing .2 pattern for second types of a denomination.

old: An Australian 50 cents from 1977, struck for Queen Elizabeth the Second's Silver Jubilee — twenty-five years on the throne. It is a big twelve-sided coin. The front shows the young Queen in Arnold Machin's famous portrait, the one Australia used through the sixties and seventies. The back is a celebration wreath: a shining starburst in the middle ringed by twenty-five little emblems, one for each year of the reign and for the states and territories of Australia, with the words SILVER JUBILEE and 50 CENTS around them. It was designed by Stuart Devlin, the goldsmith behind most of Australia's first decimal coins, and it was made to be kept — but plenty slipped into change anyway.

old: A Japanese 10 yen in bronze, dated Heisei 14 (2002), the fourteenth year of Emperor Akihito's reign. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple in Uji, a thousand-year-old building so loved that it also appears on the 10,000 yen note. The other side frames a big 10 in bay laurel. Japan has struck this design, nearly unchanged, since 1951, and it is still the 10 yen in everyday pockets today. The collection already holds two Showa-era strikes of the same design from 1982 and 1988; this is its first Heisei one.

old: Both sides photographed in the holder. Obverse reads REPUBLICA DE COSTA RICA around the arms with 2008 below; reverse reads 10 COLONES over a coffee-branch wreath, Braille dots beneath, B.C.C.R. along the bottom rim. The pale aluminium color and the round (not heptagonal) rim separate it from the collection's 1985 5 colones. The aluminium BCCR type is the only Costa Rica 10 colones struck in 2008: the brass-plated and aluminium-nickel-bronze strikes of the same design family ended in 2002, and the stainless-steel successor is dated 2021. 2008 issues were struck at Bern with the large-lettering style the photo shows; no mint mark appears on this type.
